books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, B. Advances in Technology
Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, C. Improvements in Transportation and Regional Interdependence
Transportation: Canals, Railroads, Highways, and Steamships

stimulus.text: A nineteenth-century book illustration shows Robert Fulton's steamboat Clermont at a New York dock in 1807. A large paddle wheel turns at the boat's side, smoke rises from its funnel, and workers load barrels while a crowd watches. Fulton demonstrated the boat on the Hudson River in 1807.
stimulus.source_note: Robert Fulton boards his steamboat the Clermont in New York, 1807, illustration by Louis Figuier (1819-1894), via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain; image viewed before writing. Date from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.5 B.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The steamboat in the image mattered most because it

options.text: was the first ship ever to cross the Atlantic Ocean
options.misconception: Sailing ships had crossed the Atlantic for centuries; the Clermont ran on the Hudson River, not across the ocean.

options.text: could travel upstream against the river current on a schedule
replaced the railroad as the main way to move freight
options.misconception: Railroads came later and eventually overshadowed canals and steamboats; the steamboat did not replace them.

options.text: carried enslaved laborers to the cotton fields
options.misconception: Steamboats carried freight and passengers on rivers; they were not the way enslaved people were moved to cotton fields.

rationales.A: The Atlantic had been crossed by sail since 1492. The Clermont's feat was a powered trip up the Hudson River.
rationales.B: Steam power freed river travel from wind and current. Boats could now go upstream on a timetable, and river commerce grew fast.
rationales.C: The first railroad tracks were laid in 1829, after the Clermont. Steamboats came first; railroads later took the lead.
rationales.D: The barrels and crowd in the picture show ordinary commerce. Steamboats moved freight and passengers, not enslaved field workers.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the boat. A paddle wheel and a smoking funnel mean it runs on steam, not wind.
2. Ask what steam changes on a river. A sailing vessel drifts downstream and struggles back; a steamboat goes both ways.
3. Put it together. Reliable upstream travel on a schedule is what made the steamboat matter.
Background: Within twenty years of the Clermont, steamboats dominated commercial shipping on American rivers and canals.
Remember: a new power source matters when it frees travel from wind and current.
